architecture.mechanism: Direct in-line pressure sensing of the infusion set against a calibrated occlusion threshold (20 Psi per ECRI), where a water pressure sensor detects rising upstream pressure caused by a downstream blockage and transmits the signal to a processor for real-time evaluation, with calibration accuracy quantified per device (error margins 2.84%–71.26%).
architecture.intervention: Integrate a periodically recalibrated (annual, per ECRI 20 Psi benchmark) in-line pressure sensor upstream of the patient connection whose output is continuously compared against a calibrated occlusion threshold by the pump's processor; on threshold crossing, immediately halt the pumping mechanism and trigger the occlusion alarm, with per-unit sensor error verified during calibration so the effective alarm threshold is derated by the measured sensor error margin.
architecture.expected_effect: Occlusion-induced pressure rise is detected at the sensor before the delivered volume/pressure deviation propagates to the patient, enabling alarm and pump stoppage prior to harmful medication or fluid delivery deviation; routine calibration against a dual-channel analyzer keeps sensor drift (up to ~71% error observed in uncalibrated devices) from delaying or masking detection.
architecture.falsification_test: Bench test with a syringe pump infusing water at clinical rates (e.g., 5–100 mL/h) through a test set with a programmable downstream resistance (solenoid valve or clamp) creating gradual occlusion; measure time from occlusion onset to alarm and delivered-volume deviation at alarm, before and after sensor calibration. The mechanism is falsified if any calibrated unit alarms only after pressure/volume deviation exceeds the harmful threshold, or if post-calibration sensor error exceeds the derating allowance (e.g., >5%).
